5.text: In former times sails were made of curried reindeer-

6.text: skins sewed together. Nowadays white and blue drilling is

7.text: used in the trading-villages, while in more remote places

8.text: numerous pieces of cotton and skin are patched together to

9.text: form a large sail. In rough weather, if the wind is fair,

10.text: two large floats are fastened on both sides of the boat,

11.text: below the railing; while with a side wind the boat itself is

12.text: too buoyant to allow the floats to be added. The sides of

13.text: many boats are provided also with flaps of skin or drilling,

14.text: which in rainy weather are used for covering the cargo, and

15.text: in rough weather are raised, and held in place by sticks or

16.text: simply by inverted paddles. These are very convenient, and

17.text: keep off the dashing spray even in very rough weather.

18.text: The skin boat has many advantages over the wooden

19.text: whale-boat. It is much lighter, and, while it carries more

20.text: freight, can be propelled or towed along the shore with less

21.text: labor. For the windward motion the skin boat is not so convenient, because

22.text: it is too buoyant, and, moreover, has no outer keel. Much more important

23.text: is the advantage the skin boat possesses in being able to land through heavy

24.text: surf. Both on the Arctic and on the Pacific shore the sea is very rough,

25.text: especially in the fall; and sudden squalls are frequent. The skin boat, when

26.text: caught in a storm, does not seek the harbor, but makes for the first sandy

27.text: spot free from stones, and screened from the rushing wind in some way by

28.text: coast cliffs. The landing is effected in a peculiar way: the boat, propelled

29.text: by oars, boldly makes for the shore, and in a favorable moment the end of

30.text: a rope is thrown to the shore, or, when there is nobody to catch it, a man

31.text: will jump out with it. The boat, while free on the water, is made by the

32.text: steersman to turn in alongside the shore, and then the end of another rope

33.text: is thrown from the stern, or another man jumps out with it. By pulling the

34.text: ropes tight, the men on the shore make the water side of the boat stand up

35.text: high against the breaking surf, and the first incoming wave catches the boat

36.text: — crew, cargo, and all — and casts it ashore. The flat, slippery boat acts

37.text: like a live fish; and the stronger the wave, the farther on shore will the boat

38.text: be carried. Then all the crew jump out and begin to unload, the first two

39.text: men all the time pulling the ropes, and making the boat, as it becomes

40.text: lighter and lighter, bound farther and farther toward the shore. To prevent

41.text: the skin from rubbing against the ground, oars are thrown under the boat

42.text: and secured with separate lines, so that they cannot be carried away by the
